newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Belarus leaders blasts West, wants Moscow ties.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leaders blasts West, wants Moscow ties.

text.p: Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko, preparing to take a further step in integration with Russia next week, on Friday fiercely defended his decision to expel a U.S. diplomat and his crackdown on the opposition.
Lukashenko, speaking at a news conference, accused the West of waging a slander campaign and of financing the opposition in order to disrupt his drive for union with Russia.

"We are facing a propaganda aggression against Belarus and big money is being spent on it. Its aim is to prevent a next step in the Russian-Belarussian integration," he said after a summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States in Moscow.
"In those conditions the Belarussian state takes measures to protect the people against foreign interference."
Likashenko did not name any country involved in the campaign against his rule.
But he defended the decision to expel Serzh Alexandrov, the first secretary at the U.S. embassy in Minsk, who was briefly detained at a rally against the hardline Lukashenko on Sunday.
Minsk accused him of "provocative" actions at the protest, but Washington said Alexandrov was carrying out his normal diplomatic duties by observing a political demonstration.
"Those were forced measures which every state which respects itself has to take," Lukashenko said winning applause from many top Belarussian officials who were at the news conference.
Washington retaliated by declaring as persona non grata the first secretary and consul of Belarus in the United States, Vladimir Gramyka, and giving him 24 hours to leave.
U.S. ambassador Kenneth Yalovitz was also recalled for consultations to Washington this week after Alexandrov's arrest.
The United States has told the new Belarussian ambassador not to come to Washington for some time.
Lukashenko said he was not perturbed by Washington's decision to cut $40 million in aid to Belarus over its human rights record.
"I am not going to make any concessions," he said. "My friendship with the Russians is not for sale".

Lukashenko, 42, popular with most Belarussians but hated by the small but vociferous liberal and nationalist opposition, was elected in 1994 on a campaign of closer ties with Moscow and promises to uproot corruption.

He had since clamped down on the opposition and used a landslide victory in a referendum last November to rewrite the constitution. The new basic law gave him sweeping powers and extended his term in office.

Lukashenko is pressing ahead with a closer union with Russia while accusing most of the Russian media of presenting a biased picture of events in Belarus. On Thursday Minsk ordered a reporter for the NTV commercial television network to leave the former Soviet republic in the next four days.
Kremlin insiders say Lukashenko's firm drive for integration poses a serious problem for Russian President Boris Yeltsin.
On the one hand, Lukashenko's increasingly authoritarian rule and lack of market reforms make such a union a liability.

But on the other, economic interests of many Russian enterprises in the Belarussian market as well as Minsk's strong opposition to NATO's plans to expand eastwards make such a union potentially profitable for Russia.
Yeltsin and Lukashenko signed a deal on a loose commonwealth on April 2, 1996. They are due to meet in Moscow on the anniversary of the deal to sign more integration accords.
Lukashenko said they would set up a union of equal states rather than a unitary state.
He gave few details of the deals due to be signed, but said their goal was to "bring the relations between the two states to a new level and make the integration irreversible"
